name: Gbaya
overview: A people of warrior tradition and hunters, present in several regions of Cameroon and as far as the Central African Republic, Sudan and Nigeria, the Gbaya live here alongside the Makaa of the North, the Bobilis, the Kpere, the Kako and the Bamvələ. Initiation into the labi once structured social life; today largely Christianised, they remain attached to traditional remedies and to maize beer.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group in its village, living on good terms with its neighbours; many also speak Ewondo.
Gbaya is spoken in several regions (Adamawa, North, East, Centre, South) and, beyond, in the Central African Republic, Sudan and Nigeria.
People formerly married among the Gbaya; today, they marry whom they like.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land, with purely Gbaya neighbourhoods; other groups have joined them there.
Tradition has the Gbaya coming from Egypt, through Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Every two years, the mɔinam brings together all the Gbaya.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Patriarchal society: decisions are made within the family and it is the father who decides.
One inherits within one's own clan; daughters' children do not inherit.
Men's and women's societies passed down from generation to generation: the initiates and those in charge of widowhood rites.
Children greet first; the wife does not look her husband in the eye, which would be contempt.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife settles with her husband.
The boy becomes a man through initiation into the labi; for the girl, her behaviour and maturity are observed.
Formerly, a girl was sometimes promised from birth to seal a friendship.
It is the young man's aunts who make the first move; it also happened that a girl went of her own accord to live with her suitor.

No bride price in money: the conduct of the son-in-law is observed. The symbolic gifts are a chicken, a spear, a mat and a knife, emblems of a warrior people; offering others would bring misfortune on the couple's children.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Some families perform an ancestral rite when a woman is pregnant, even far from the village.
A child who is born is welcomed as a warrior, a fighter.
Death mobilises the whole community, which seeks its causes (ndoŋ awù).
The former sacred places have mostly disappeared; yet a mystical rock announces bereavements.

Incest taboo. Prohibitions: the child gives his first game to his father; men eat neither leopard (kɔ́yɔ́) nor wild boar entrails, which they hand over to their parents in exchange for their blessing.
Killing, even in war, requires a purification rite; theft is a serious offence.
Divination by lightning, leaves and barks, the spoken word (curse).

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: hunting, land clearing, livestock rearing. Women: ploughing, sowing, harvesting, trade.
The land belongs to everyone; each person farms the plots inherited from their parents.
Craftsmanship was formerly organised in castes, now disappeared.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Old clothing of woven bark (ndumbu) and of leaves (yakɛdɛ), then saro, gandoura and wrappers.
Distrust of the hospital: many trust plants and healers.
Beauty: scars, filed teeth, musculature and a fine voice for men; tattoos and filed teeth for women.
Courtship: good hunter, drummer, good singer, exemplary conduct; for the woman, tattoos, conduct and vigilance.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: labi (vigorous, linked to initiation), patenge, yɔŋgɔ, kɛkɛ, awunda, on the drum (bīo).
The yaorop is danced at deaths; the tabi at the end of initiation or at the death of an initiate.
The festivals of the harvests, of the return of the rains and of the start of the dry season are no longer practised.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The absence of bride price in some families and the distrust of the hospital set the Gbaya apart, who resemble the Centre and South groups in other respects.

sections.title: The names
items: Twins' names: Ngozo and Yabub for boys, Toza and Zeri for girls.
The names of the deceased are given again so that they do not disappear; the name does not change.
Certain names are not pronounced, on pain of a fine; one says dâ (the father) and na (the mother).
The founding ancestor, Mbartoua, is “the one who blocks the door”.

lessons.title: Who are the Gbaya? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Gbaya community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Gbaya community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Gbaya community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Gbaya community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Gbaya community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Gbaya call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Group in the majority in its village, living on good terms with its neighbours; many also speak Ewondo. • Gbaya is spoken in several regions (Adamawa, North, East, Centre, South) and, beyond, in the Central African Republic, Sudan and Nigeria. • In the past, people married among Gbaya; today, they marry whomever they like. • Ancestral land, with purely Gbaya neighbourhoods; other groups have joined them. • Tradition says the Gbaya came from Egypt, through Sudan and the Central African Republic.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A people of warrior tradition and hunters, present in several regions of Cameroon and as far as the Central African Republic, Sudan and Nigeria, the Gbaya live here alongside the Makaa of the North, the Bobilis, the Kpere, the Kako and the Bamvələ. Initiation into the labi once structured social life; today largely Christianised, they remain attached to traditional remedies and to maize beer.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Gbaya community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Gbaya organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Gbaya village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Gbaya organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Gbaya village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Patriarchal society: decisions are taken within the family and the father has the final say. • One inherits within one's own clan; daughters' children do not inherit. • Men's and women's societies handed down from generation to generation: the initiates and those in charge of widowhood rites. • Children greet first; the wife does not look her husband in the eyes, as this would be contempt.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Patriarchal society: decisions are taken within the family and the father has the final say. People inherit within their own clan; daughters' children do not inherit. Men's and women's societies passed down from generation to generation: the initiates and those in charge of widowhood rites.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Gbaya, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Gbaya
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Gbaya, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Gbaya.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Gbaya, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Gbaya.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: cassava couscous, salt-and-chilli sauce (tɔ́ŋ nɛ ndónge). • Drinks: ndolo / kpata (maize beer). • Men: hunting, clearing land, livestock rearing. Women: tilling, sowing, harvesting, trade.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Gbaya eat mainly cassava couscous, tɔ́ŋ nɛ ndónge. Traditional drinks: maize beer. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Gbaya: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Gbaya
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth

objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments

student.intro: Discover the music and dances of the Gbaya, then learn to perform one.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: List the dances and say on what occasion each one is performed.

activities.title: I describe
activities.instruction: Choose the most representative dance: participants, instruments, attire, gestures.

activities.title: I understand
activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Gbaya, traditional dances (deaths, tabi) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum. Festival(s): mɔinam.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Gbaya
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Gbaya, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Gbaya. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Gbaya, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Gbaya. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men: hunting, clearing, livestock. Women: ploughing, sowing, harvesting, trade. • Land belongs to everyone; each person farms the plots inherited from their parents. • Crafts were formerly organised in castes, now disappeared.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: hunting, land clearing, livestock rearing. Women: ploughing, sowing, harvesting, trade. Land belongs to everyone; each person farms the plots inherited from their parents.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Gbaya's activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I classify

activities.title: I calculate

activities.title: I propose

student.memo: Men: hunting, land clearing, livestock rearing. Women: ploughing, sowing, harvesting, trade. Land belongs to everyone; each person farms the plots inherited from their parents.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Gbaya
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Gbaya, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Gbaya. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Gbaya, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Gbaya. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Certain families perform an ancestral rite when a woman is pregnant, even far from the village. • The child who is born is welcomed as a warrior, a fighter. • Death mobilises the whole community, which seeks out its causes (ndoŋ awù). • Most of the old sacred places have disappeared; yet a mystical rock announces deaths. • Taboo of incest. Prohibitions: the child gives their first game to their father; men eat neither panther (kɔ́yɔ́) nor wild boar entrails, which they hand over to their parents in exchange for their blessing.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Some families perform an ancestral rite when a woman is pregnant, even far from the village. The child who is born is welcomed as a warrior, a fighter.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Gbaya (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Gbaya believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify

activities.title: I explain

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: Some families perform an ancestral rite when a woman is pregnant, even far from the village. The child who is born is welcomed as a warrior, a fighter.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Gbaya and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Gbaya family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Gbaya greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Gbaya family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Gbaya. • Greetings: Mosamɛ = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Mɛ nɛ = morning greeting (one person); Mosa enɛ = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Pɔ̍k, Yίto, Tar, Nar, Mɔrɔ. • The founding ancestor, Mbartoua, is “the one who blocks the door”. • The absence of bride price in some families and the distrust of hospitals single out the Gbaya, who resemble the groups of the Centre and South in other respects.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Gbaya are the first steps towards communicating with the Gbaya. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Gbaya.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Gbaya are the first steps towards communicating with the Gbaya. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
